doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: The stand-up bass and the rhythm section
summary: Hunter and Rowe discuss the warmth of the upright bass and Bill Doggett's bass pedals.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: So the James Hunter Six has this, in my opinion, has this identifiable sound. And I think part of it is because you’re still playing with a stand up bass.
Yeah I think probably. It has a certain warmth to it you know, and it was a shame it disappeared entirely for a while in popular music.
Yeah. And it doesn’t dominate the music like an electric bass can.

No that’s right. You know like basically a rhythm section in a record appeals to me it sort of just sits in the pocket and drives it along and sometimes you’re not that conscious of it being there, you just feel it. It’s very much the case, a good example is somebody like Bill Doggett, whose contributions to his own records aren’t always readily sort of apparent but he’s there driving it from underneath with the bass pedals making it sort of throb along. And you can’t hear what he’s doing but you can feel it.
Exactly. You go to put that, you go okay what key is he in and you put your ear closer to the speaker to pick out those bass notes.
It’s nice if you have to look for it, yeah.
